summary: This is Snowflake documentation for the GET command, which downloads files from a Snowflake internal stage (named stage, table stage, or user stage) to a local directory on a client machine. It covers the syntax, required parameters (internalStage and file:// local path with Linux/macOS and Windows formatting rules), optional PARALLEL and PATTERN parameters, usage notes such as lack of support for external stages and no preservation of directory structure, and examples.
one_line: Snowflake reference for the GET command, which downloads files from internal stages to a client machine's local directory.
key_facts: The GET command downloads files from Snowflake internal stages to a local directory or folder on a client machine.
Supported internal stage types for GET are a named internal stage, an internal stage for a specified table, and an internal stage for the current user.
GET can be used to download data files after unloading data from a table using the COPY INTO location command.
The PARALLEL parameter sets the number of threads used for downloading, with supported values from 1 to 99.
The default value of PARALLEL is 10.
The PATTERN parameter takes a regular expression to filter files; by default all files in the specified stage are downloaded.
GET does not support downloading files from external stages; users must use utilities provided by their cloud service for that.
GET does not preserve stage directory structure when transferring files to the client machine.
The GET command does not rename files.
On Linux/macOS the local path must include the initial forward slash, for example file:///tmp/load.
On Windows the path must include the drive and backslash, for example file://C:temp/load, and enclosed URIs use forward slashes such as 'file://C:/temp/load data'.
If a filename is specified as part of the local path, the JDBC or ODBC driver creates a subdirectory with that filename instead of saving a file.
Example: GET @%mytable file:///tmp/data/; downloads all files in the stage for the mytable table to /tmp/data.
